title: Car Maintenance for Beginners: 8 Checks to Do Yourself
hook: You don't need to be a mechanic to keep your car safe and reliable. Eight simple checks, done once a month, can catch problems early and save you hundreds on repairs. Here's how to do each one in minutes, with no special tools and no jacks. It's easier than you think. We also cover what to do when a reading looks wrong.
intro: Regular checks are the cheapest insurance for your car. Every check in this video is visual, or takes a single simple tool. We won't touch brakes, jack up the car or work on anything that could be dangerous. Park on level ground, switch off the engine, put the handbrake on, and keep your owner's manual nearby, because it shows exactly where everything is located on your model. Set a reminder on the first weekend of each month, and the whole routine takes about twenty minutes.
youNeed: A clean rag or paper towel
A coin for the tread test
youNeedNarration: Here's what you need. Your owner's manual, which is the most useful tool of all. A tire pressure gauge. A clean rag or paper towel. A coin for checking tire tread. And a flashlight, in case the light is dim. If you don't have a gauge, they cost just a few dollars at any auto shop. Everything fits in a small box in the trunk.
heroImagePrompt: A person in casual clothes looking at the open hood of a parked car in a driveway, morning light, shallow depth of field, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Check tire pressure
steps.narration: Step one. Check your tires when they are cold, before driving or after the car has stood for a few hours. Find the correct pressure on the sticker inside the driver's door frame, not on the tire's side wall, which shows the maximum. Unscrew the valve cap, press the gauge on firmly, and read the number. Add air at a gas station if it's low. Correct pressure improves safety, fuel economy and tire life. Check all four tires, and the spare if you have one. If you are unsure, fill a little at a time and recheck. Never fill past the maximum number.
steps.tip: Use the door sticker, not the sidewall
steps.mistake: Checking pressure after a long drive
steps.imagePrompt: A hand pressing a tire pressure gauge onto the valve of a car wheel, close-up, daylight, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Inspect your tire tread
steps.narration: Step two. Tires with worn tread grip badly, especially in rain. Place a coin into the main groove of the tire. In many places the legal minimum is two thirty-seconds of an inch, or one point six millimetres, and a coin can help you judge it. If the tread covers part of the coin's edge, you still have some life left. If you can see all of it, the tire needs replacing soon. Also look for cracks, bulges, nails and uneven wear. If you see a wear indicator bar, a small raised bar in the groove, that tells you the legal limit has been reached.
steps.tip: Check several spots across each tire
steps.mistake: Ignoring bulges or cracks in the rubber
steps.imagePrompt: A coin placed in the tread groove of a car tire to check wear, close-up, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Check the engine oil
steps.narration: Step three. With the car on level ground and the engine off for at least five minutes, open the hood and find the dipstick, which usually has a bright yellow or orange handle. Pull it out, wipe it with a rag, push it fully back in, and pull it out again. The oil should be between the two marks. Healthy oil is amber to brown. If it's very low, add the oil type listed in your manual, a little at a time. Keep a clean rag in the car, since a stained dipstick can be hard to read in dim light.
steps.mistake: Adding the wrong type of oil
steps.imagePrompt: A hand pulling an oil dipstick with amber oil on it from a car engine, close-up, bright light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Look at the coolant level
steps.narration: Step four. Coolant keeps your engine from overheating. Find the translucent reservoir under the hood, which has minimum and maximum marks, and check the level while the engine is cold. Never open the radiator or reservoir cap on a hot engine, because pressurized hot liquid can cause serious burns. If the level is below minimum, top it up with the coolant type that your manual specifies. A level that keeps dropping may mean a leak, so see a mechanic. Keep the cap tightly closed afterward, and wipe any spills off the plastic and the paint.
steps.tip: Only open the cap on a cold engine
steps.mistake: Opening the cap on a hot engine
steps.imagePrompt: A translucent coolant reservoir with minimum and maximum marks inside a clean car engine bay, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Top up washer fluid, check wipers
steps.narration: Step five. Open the cap marked with a windshield symbol and fill the washer fluid reservoir with proper washer fluid, not plain water, especially in cold weather. Then run your fingers along each wiper blade and look for cracks, splits or a hardened edge. Test them with the washer spray. If they chatter, streak or squeak, replace them. Wiper blades are cheap, simple to change, and an important safety feature when visibility drops in the rain. Washer fluid with antifreeze protects the system in freezing weather, so choose one for your climate.
steps.mistake: Filling the reservoir with plain water in winter
steps.imagePrompt: A hand pouring blue windshield washer fluid into a car's reservoir with a funnel, bright light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Test all your lights
steps.narration: Step six. Park facing a wall or a shop window and switch on your headlights, then the high beams, the indicators, the hazard lights and the fog lights. Have a friend stand behind the car while you press the brake pedal, to check the brake lights, and engage reverse for the reversing lights. Don't forget the license plate light. A bulb that has failed is a safety risk and, in many places, a fine. Most bulbs are cheap and easy to replace. Replace a failed bulb in pairs when you can, because the second one is usually close to the end of its life.
steps.tip: Ask a friend to check the rear lights
steps.mistake: Driving with a dead brake light
steps.imagePrompt: A parked car with its headlights switched on facing a dark garage wall, glowing beams, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Look over the battery
steps.narration: Step seven. Open the hood and look at the battery. The terminals, the metal connectors on top, should be clean and tight. White, blue or green crusty powder is corrosion, which can prevent the car from starting. The case should not be swollen or leaking. Do not touch the terminals with metal tools. If you see corrosion or if the engine is slow to start, ask a garage to clean it and test the battery. Batteries typically last three to five years. Never smoke or use flames near a battery, because it can release flammable gas.
steps.tip: A slow start is an early warning
steps.imagePrompt: A close-up of a car battery with clean metal terminals and red and black cables, engine bay, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Read the dashboard and manual
steps.narration: Step eight. When you start the car, watch the dashboard. Warning lights should come on briefly, then switch off. A light that stays on, especially red ones for oil pressure, battery or temperature, means you should stop safely and call for help. Amber lights, such as the check engine light, mean you should get the car looked at soon. Open your manual to the maintenance schedule, and mark the dates for oil changes and inspections.
steps.mistake: Ignoring a warning light for weeks
steps.imagePrompt: A car dashboard instrument cluster with a few illuminated warning symbols, close-up, soft light, photorealistic, no text

bonus.label: TROUBLESHOOTING
bonus.title: When a reading looks wrong
bonus.narration: If a reading looks odd, check it again before you worry. Cold weather lowers tire pressure, so a warning light on the first cold morning often just needs air. Oil that looks dark is not automatically bad, because oil darkens as it works. Milky oil, or an oily film in the coolant, means stop driving and call a mechanic.
bonus.tip: Milky oil means stop and call
bonus.imagePrompt: A hand holding a car dipstick wiped on a white rag to show a thin line of amber oil, the open hood of a car blurred in the background, daylight. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: CALL A PRO
bonus.title: When to call a mechanic
bonus.narration: A red warning light, or a temperature needle rising into the red, means pull over safely and switch the engine off. Grinding or squealing when you brake, or a car that pulls to one side, needs a professional. A puddle under the car, or a burning smell, is another reason to call.
bonus.imagePrompt: A mechanic in blue coveralls looking at the open hood of a car in a bright garage, a rolling tool cart in the background, seen from behind so no face is visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: PREVENTION
bonus.title: Make it a monthly habit
bonus.narration: Pick one day each month, like the first Saturday, and set a reminder on your phone. Write each reading in a notes app, so you can spot changes. Follow the service schedule in your manual for oil changes and tire rotation.
bonus.imagePrompt: An open car glove box holding a tire pressure gauge, a folded rag, a small flashlight and an owner's manual, neatly arranged, interior light. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Here are three mistakes beginners make. First, checking fluids on a hot engine or on sloping ground. The readings will be wrong, and hot coolant is dangerous. Second, ignoring small warnings. A dim light, a low reading or a strange noise is much cheaper to fix early. And third, trying to do jobs beyond your experience, like working under a car or on the brakes. For those, always use a professional. Write the date of each check in your phone, so that you can spot changes over time.
items: Checking fluids on a hot engine
Working under the car or on brakes

recap.narration: Let's recap. Check your tire pressure. Inspect the tread. Check the engine oil. Look at the coolant level. Top up the washer fluid and check the wipers. Test all your lights. Look over the battery. And read the dashboard and your manual. Eight quick checks, once a month, and your car will be safer and cheaper to run. If a reading looks wrong, double-check it, and call a mechanic for red warnings.
items: Top up washer fluid, check wipers

outro: That's eight car checks anyone can do. If this helped, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments what kind of car you drive, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow, and drive safely.

metadata.title: Car Maintenance for Beginners: 8 Checks to Do Yourself
metadata.description:
New to cars? In this step-by-step video you'll learn car maintenance for beginners: eight simple checks you can do yourself in minutes. We cover tire pressure and tread, engine oil, coolant, washer fluid and wipers, lights, the battery, and dashboard warning lights. No jacks, no brakes and no special tools. Just visual checks and levels, done safely on level ground with the engine off.

You'll need: your owner's manual, a tire pressure gauge, a clean rag or paper towel, a coin for the tread test, a flashlight.
